messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Vignette:
Vannak is a 47-year-old Cambodian American man who has spent most of his adult life working outdoors as a park ranger, a job he once described as steadying because the trails, weather patterns, and daily routines felt knowable. He is married and the father of a child whose sudden, life-threatening illness changed the texture of ordinary life for him. When he talks about that period, he returns first to the hospital itself: the sharp antiseptic smell at the entrance, the rubbing alcohol on gloved hands, the chemical odor that seemed to cling to his clothes even after he got home. His child had become critically ill quickly enough that there had been no sense of preparation. He remembers moving through bright hallways with a feeling that everything was happening too fast, then standing still beside the bed while monitors sounded and staff moved in and out using language he could not fully take in. What has stayed with him is the helplessness of watching his child’s body in danger while others controlled what happened next.

In the weeks after the medical crisis, Vannak found that certain sensations could pull him back into that atmosphere with unnerving force. If he felt lightheaded while walking a trail in the summer heat, he did not experience it as a passing physical sensation. The dizziness itself frightened him. For a moment he would be back in that suspended state of waiting, scanning for signs that something catastrophic was about to happen. The smell of antiseptic was even more immediate. As a park ranger, he sometimes passed the first-aid station or opened supply cabinets stocked with disinfectant, and the odor would hit him before he had time to prepare. He would stiffen, lose the thread of whatever he had been doing, and feel as if the hospital had suddenly intruded on the park. The smell of alcohol could have a similar effect. Even something mundane, like sanitizer left out at a visitor center or the trace of alcohol on someone’s breath during an interaction, could unsettle him.

Over time, he also became preoccupied with the actions of other people during his child’s illness. He dwells on what others did to him and his family, turning over perceived failures and offenses with a repetitive, embittered focus. In session he speaks at length about who should have acted sooner, who did not listen properly, who did not understand the seriousness quickly enough. He can spend hours replaying exchanges in his mind, returning to the same points and imagining how to get even with the people he believes wronged them. Although the original trauma was his child’s illness, his mind has become crowded with fantasies of confrontation and retaliation toward those he holds responsible for adding to the family’s suffering. He is certain that other people’s actions cannot simply be left alone; to him, their part in what happened feels unfinished, intolerable, and morally charged.

Because of this, Vannak has become wary when other people bring up the event. He avoids reminders when they come through conversation, changing the subject when relatives ask about that time or leaving the room if his wife starts to talk about the hospital. At work he keeps interactions practical and brief. If a coworker mentions a child’s emergency or a medical scare, he will find a reason to step away, check a trail report, or return to his truck. This has had visible consequences. His wife experiences him as absent when family members try to make sense of what happened together, and he has become more cut off at home. In the park, colleagues know him as reliable but increasingly closed off; he no longer lingers in the ranger station when conversation turns personal.

By the time he sought help, these patterns had narrowed his life considerably. He was tired of feeling ambushed by smells and bodily sensations in the middle of a workday, and tired of how quickly his thoughts would turn toward blame and revenge. What finally brought him in was not a single dramatic incident but an accumulation of moments: feeling dizzy on patrol and needing to stop; catching the smell of disinfectant in the visitor center and losing his focus; going home tense and silent while his wife tried, again, to talk about their child’s illness. He says he wants some way to be in the same world as these reminders without feeling pulled back into that hospital, and without his mind filling so quickly with what other people did wrong. What frightens him most is that he has begun to live as if those days are still waiting for him somewhere, ready to break through the present at the smallest cue.
